title: Saturn has a hexagon at its north pole, each side longer than Earth is wide

cover.alt: Cassini’s view of Saturn’s sunlit north pole, with the six-sided jet stream circling the central polar vortex.

body: A jet stream around Saturn’s north pole, at about 78° N, flows in a nearly perfect hexagon. Each side is about **14,500 km** long, roughly 2,000 km more than Earth’s diameter, and the winds in it blow at around 320 km/h. Voyager photographed it in 1981, Cassini watched it again from 2006, and it rotates once every 10 h 39 min 24 s, the same period as radio emissions from Saturn’s interior, without ever drifting in longitude. In laboratory tanks of spinning fluid, shear between fast and slow bands produces the same kind of polygon, most often with six sides.

slides.heading: Compared with Earth, in kilometres
slides.note: Earth’s equatorial diameter is 12,756 km; the hexagon is also about 300 km tall

slides.label: one rotation of the hexagon, the same as Saturn’s radio period
slides.text: Unlike the clouds around it, the hexagon does not shift in longitude, which suggests it is tied to the planet’s deep rotation.

slides.question: How fast do the winds in the hexagon’s jet stream blow?
slides.explanation: Around 320 km/h. The jet is about 300 km high and the whole six-sided pattern turns once every 10 h 39 min 24 s.

slides.heading: Made in a tank
slides.text: Scientists spun a circular tank of liquid with its centre and its edge moving at different speeds. The shear between the two produced similar polygons: six sides was the most common, though shapes with three to eight sides appeared too.

slides.question: What does the hexagon’s rotation period match?
slides.explanation: It turns once every 10 h 39 min 24 s, the same period as the radio emissions from Saturn’s interior, which is why it is thought to track the planet’s deep rotation.
